reference.source: Stiehm's Immune Deficiencies / Middleton's Allergy: Principles and Practice
clinicalPearls: The signature clinical association is recurrent invasive Neisseria infection, especially meningococcal disease and disseminated gonococcal infection
Meningococcal disease in these patients is often caused by uncommon serogroups and may recur or present at an atypical age
Inheritance is autosomal recessive, so consanguinity or affected siblings increase suspicion
The defect lies in assembling the membrane attack complex, so bacteriolysis of Neisseria is impaired despite otherwise intact immunity
A low CH50 (classical pathway) with normal individual early components points to a terminal pathway defect and should trigger measurement of individual terminal components
Properdin deficiency (X-linked) and early complement defects can produce overlapping neisserial susceptibility and should be considered
Prevention centres on meningococcal vaccination including serogroup B and quadrivalent conjugate vaccines, and prompt treatment of febrile illness
reference.pathophysiology: The terminal complement components C5 through C9 assemble on microbial surfaces to form the membrane attack complex, a pore that lyses susceptible organisms. Neisseria species are unusually dependent on this direct complement-mediated bacteriolysis for their clearance. When any terminal component is genetically deficient, the classical, lectin and alternative pathways can still opsonise but cannot complete lytic killing, so the host is left disproportionately vulnerable to Neisseria meningitidis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae. Because early complement functions such as opsonisation and immune-complex handling are preserved, patients typically do not have the encapsulated-organism infection pattern or autoimmune features seen with early classical pathway defects.
additionalDifferentials: Early classical pathway component deficiency (C1, C2, C4)
Factor D or other alternative pathway defects
Antibody deficiency predisposing to bacterial infection
Complement consumption from active immune-complex disease
additionalInvestigations: CH50 (total classical haemolytic complement) as a screen for terminal pathway integrity
AH50 (alternative pathway haemolytic assay) to help localise the defect
Measurement of individual terminal components C5 to C9
Properdin and early component (C3, C4, C2) levels to exclude other complement defects
Microbiological culture and serogrouping of any neisserial isolate
Genetic confirmation of the deficient component where available
redFlags: Recurrent or second episode of invasive meningococcal disease
Meningococcal infection caused by an unusual serogroup or occurring in an adolescent/adult
Family history of invasive neisserial infection or unexplained meningitis deaths
Fulminant sepsis with purpura requiring immediate treatment
reference.prognosis: Individual invasive episodes tend to be less fulminant than in complement-sufficient patients, but the lifelong risk of recurrent neisserial infection persists, and outcome depends heavily on vaccination, patient education, and rapid treatment of febrile illness.
pitfalls: Attributing a single meningococcal episode to bad luck and not screening the complement system after recurrent or atypical disease
Measuring only individual components without a functional CH50/AH50 to guide localisation
Assuming vaccination gives complete protection and failing to counsel on urgent care for fevers
Overlooking properdin deficiency, which mimics the neisserial phenotype
management: Prioritise immunisation against Neisseria meningitidis with both quadrivalent conjugate (MenACWY) and serogroup B vaccines, with boosters, as the cornerstone of prevention
Complete vaccination against other encapsulated organisms including pneumococcus and Haemophilus influenzae type b
Consider long-term prophylactic penicillin to reduce the risk of invasive meningococcal disease
Educate the patient to seek urgent medical care for any febrile illness and to carry an alert document, given the lifelong recurrent-infection risk
Treat suspected invasive meningococcal or gonococcal infection promptly with a third-generation cephalosporin such as ceftriaxone
Screen and vaccinate at-risk family members and offer genetic counselling for this autosomal recessive defect
Provide ongoing clinical immunology follow-up and culture and serogroup any neisserial isolate to guide public-health action
